posts.title: MOOWR in simple words: pay customs duty later, not at the port
posts.excerpt: A plain explanation of the scheme, with an example, for anyone who imports and manufactures in India.
posts.body:
Normally, when you bring goods into India, you pay customs duty at the port before you can take them out. For a factory that imports machines or raw materials, that is a large amount of cash paid long before any product is made or sold.

MOOWR is a scheme that lets you pay that duty later. The name stands for Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations, 2019. It works under section 65 of the Customs Act, 1962.

## The idea in one line

You keep your imported goods in a customs-approved warehouse (a bonded warehouse), do your manufacturing there, and pay duty only when the goods leave for sale in India.

## A simple example

A company imports a machine and some raw material. Without the scheme, it pays duty on both at the port, then waits months to earn money from the product. With the scheme, the goods go into the bonded warehouse without duty at that stage. The company makes its product. If it sells in India, duty is paid when the goods leave the warehouse. If it exports, no import duty is charged on the imported goods used.

## Who it helps

- Factories that import machinery or raw materials
- Businesses that export a large part of what they make
- Businesses that want to keep cash for running the business instead of locking it in duty

## What you need to do

- Apply to the customs authority for permission and a licence for the warehouse
- Give a bond, which is a written promise to follow the rules and pay any duty that falls due
- Keep clear records of what comes in, what is used, what is made, and what goes out
- Send the returns and records that customs asks for, on time

## Things to think about first

- Duty is put off, not removed. Goods sold in India will still attract duty.
- The records are the heart of the scheme. Poor records can cause trouble later.
- The rules and how customs applies them change from time to time, so check the current position before you apply.
- It does not suit every business. It depends on what you import, what you make, and how much you sell in India and abroad.

## Is it right for you?

Whether MOOWR suits a business depends on what it imports, what it makes, and how much it sells in India and abroad. The official text is available in the Reading material section of this website.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: EMI scheme in simple words: pay customs duty once a month
posts.excerpt: How the Eligible Manufacturer Importer facility lets approved manufacturers pay import duty monthly instead of at every clearance.
posts.body:
Normally, an importer pays customs duty on each consignment before the goods leave the port. For a factory that imports every week, that means paying duty again and again, often long before the finished product is sold.

The Eligible Manufacturer Importer (EMI) facility changes this for approved manufacturers. They can clear goods without paying duty at that moment, and pay the duty for all clearances together once a month.

## The basics

- It was introduced by CBIC Circular No. 08/2026-Customs, dated 28 February 2026.
- It works under the Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016.
- It is available from 1 April 2026 and stays in force until 31 March 2028.

## A simple example

A manufacturer imports components on several dates in a month. Without the facility, it pays duty on every Bill of Entry at the time of clearance. As an approved EMI, it clears all the shipments first, and pays the total duty by the 1st of the next month. For goods cleared in March, the payment is due by 31 March.

## Who can apply

The circular sets conditions on compliance, turnover, financial standing and track record. As reported, the main ones include:

- A valid Importer-Exporter Code and registration as a manufacturer under GST.
- A minimum number of import or export documents in the previous year (fewer for MSMEs).
- Turnover above a stated limit, and at least two years in business.
- GST returns filed, no unpaid tax collected, and a clean record under customs and tax laws.
- A Chartered Accountant's certificate showing financial soundness.

Existing AEO Tier 1 entities that meet these conditions can also apply. The circular itself has the full list and the exact figures.

## How it works

1. The application is made online on the AEO portal, under the Eligible Manufacturer Importer tab.
2. The Directorate of International Customs reviews it.
3. After approval, the status is updated in the customs system.
4. A nominated person gets an ICEGATE login to authenticate transactions.
5. On each Bill of Entry, the importer selects the deferred payment option and authenticates it with an OTP.

## Things to keep in mind

- The duty is deferred, not waived. It must be paid by the due date every month.
- The conditions must be met throughout the period. If they are not, or if payment is missed, the approval can be suspended or withdrawn.
- Circulars and portal procedures can change, so the current text should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: EPCG scheme in simple words: import machinery without customs duty
posts.excerpt: What the Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme is, how the export obligation works, and what happens at the end.
posts.body:
A factory that wants to start exporting often needs new machinery, and importing it means paying customs duty. The Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) scheme helps with that cost. It is run by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) under the Foreign Trade Policy.

## The idea in one line

You import capital goods at zero customs duty, and in return you promise to export a set value of goods within a set time.

## How the promise works

The promise is called the export obligation. Under Foreign Trade Policy 2023, it is generally:

- 6 times the duty saved,
- to be fulfilled within 6 years from the date of the authorisation.

A lower multiple applies in some cases, for example when the capital goods are bought from an Indian manufacturer. A separate average export obligation can also apply, so the authorisation itself should always be read closely.

## A simple example

Suppose the customs duty on a machine would normally be Rs 10 lakh. Under EPCG, the duty is not paid, so the duty saved is Rs 10 lakh. The exporter must then export goods worth 6 times that, which is Rs 60 lakh, within 6 years.

## Who can apply

- Manufacturer exporters
- Merchant exporters tied to a supporting manufacturer
- Service providers who earn foreign exchange

All of them need a valid Importer-Exporter Code (IEC).

## How to apply

- The application is filed online on the DGFT portal, before the import.
- It needs supporting papers, such as a Chartered Engineer's certificate for the machinery.
- When the goods are imported, customs takes a bond or other security for the duty saved.

## What happens at the end

The exporter submits proof of exports and realised foreign exchange. DGFT then issues the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate (EODC), which closes the authorisation.

If the obligation is not fulfilled, the duty saved on the unfulfilled part has to be paid back with interest. Extensions are possible in some cases, but the liability remains.

## Keep in mind

DGFT issues public notices from time to time that change deadlines, procedures and facilities for EPCG. The current notices and the Handbook of Procedures should be checked before acting.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: EPR in simple words: what importers should know about Extended Producer Responsibility
posts.excerpt: What EPR means, which products it covers, and why it now matters at the customs counter.
posts.body:
When a product reaches the end of its life, someone has to collect and recycle it. Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) puts that duty on the businesses that put the product on the market: the producers, brand owners and importers.

## What EPR means

A business covered by EPR has to register with the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) through its online portal. It must then make sure a set share of its products is collected and recycled, usually through registered recyclers, and report this every year.

## Which products are covered

Each type of product has its own rules:

- Plastic packaging: the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, as amended.
- Electrical and electronic equipment: the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022.
- Batteries: the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022.
- Other rules cover items such as waste tyres and used oil.

## Why it matters to importers

An importer counts as a producer. If a business imports goods that fall under these rules and sells them in India, it has to register, even if it does not make anything in India.

Customs also looks at this now:

- For plastic, a CPCB direction dated 13 June 2025 asks importers of plastic packaging and of plastic raw material meant for packaging to register on the EPR portal. Customs has been asked to check for the registration before clearing such consignments.
- For electronic goods, customs can ask for proof of EPR registration, or a declaration, before clearance.

## What registration involves

- An account on the CPCB portal, using the business's IEC, PAN and GST details.
- Documents about the products imported and sold.
- For electronics, agreements with authorised recyclers and an EPR plan.
- Yearly returns showing that targets were met.

## Practical points

- Check whether the product's customs tariff heading falls under any of these rules.
- Register before the goods arrive, because clearance can be held up without it.
- Keep records of quantities imported and sold, since annual returns depend on them.

The rules and portal requirements are updated often, so the current CPCB notifications should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: RoDTEP in simple words: getting back the hidden taxes on exports
posts.excerpt: What the Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products scheme refunds, how the refund is given, and how it is claimed.
posts.body:
When goods are made in India, taxes get built into the cost along the way: on fuel, on electricity, on documents. Some of these are not refunded under any other scheme. The Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products (RoDTEP) scheme gives that burden back to exporters, so that taxes are not exported along with the goods.

## What it refunds

RoDTEP covers central, state and local duties and taxes that are not refunded elsewhere. Examples include taxes on fuel used in transport, duty on electricity, mandi tax and stamp duty on export documents.

## How the refund is given

- The refund is not paid in cash.
- It is given as an electronic credit, called a scrip, in the exporter's ICEGATE account.
- The scrip can be used to pay basic customs duty, or transferred to someone else who can use it.

## How much

The refund is a percentage of the value of the exported goods, and some items have a cap on the value per unit. The rates are listed item by item in a schedule. If a product is not in the schedule, it does not get RoDTEP.

## Who can claim

Exporters of goods that appear in the notified schedule. A few goods are excluded, such as pan masala and tobacco products. Exports from SEZs and EOUs have separate provisions.

## How to claim

1. When filing the shipping bill, the exporter selects the RoDTEP option and the correct item code.
2. Customs checks the claim after the export, through its system.
3. If it is accepted, the scrip is credited to the ICEGATE account.

The claim has to be made at the shipping bill stage. A missed declaration may rule out a claim later.

## How long it runs

RoDTEP is extended in short periods. DGFT Notification No. 41/2026-27, dated 30 September 2026, continues it up to 31 December 2026 for exports from DTA units, Advance Authorisation holders, SEZ units and EOUs. The rates and caps stay the same during the extension. Because it has been extended several times, the latest notification should be checked.

## RoDTEP and drawback

Duty drawback refunds customs duty paid on imported inputs. RoDTEP covers different taxes. Whether both can be claimed on the same goods depends on the rules for that product, so this needs checking case by case.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Advance Authorisation in simple words: import inputs without duty to make export goods
posts.excerpt: How the scheme works, the export obligation and value addition, and what happens if the promise is not kept.
posts.body:
A manufacturer who exports often imports raw material or components to make the goods. Paying customs duty on those inputs, and then waiting for a refund, ties up money. Advance Authorisation lets the exporter import the inputs without paying that duty, as long as the inputs go into goods that are exported.

It is issued by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) under the Foreign Trade Policy.

## What is exempted

The authorisation exempts the basic customs duty and other customs duties on the inputs, along with Integrated Tax (IGST) and compensation cess.

## The promise

In return, the holder takes on an export obligation:

- The inputs must be used to make products that are exported.
- The export obligation period is 18 months from the date the authorisation is issued.
- The exports must carry at least 15% value addition.

How much input can be imported for each unit of export is set by the Standard Input Output Norms (SION). Where there is no standard norm, the holder applies for one.

## A simple example

An exporter plans to export shirts. It gets an authorisation for the fabric needed, imports the fabric without paying duty, makes the shirts, and exports them. The fabric must go into the exported shirts, and it cannot be sold in India.

## Who can apply

- Manufacturer exporters
- Merchant exporters tied to a supporting manufacturer
- Certain suppliers for deemed exports

A valid Importer-Exporter Code (IEC) is needed.

## The process

1. The application is filed on the DGFT portal.
2. After approval, the holder gives customs a bond, bank guarantee or similar security.
3. The inputs must be imported within the validity of the authorisation, which is 12 months from issue, with one extension of up to 12 months in some cases.
4. After exporting, the holder applies for the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate (EODC), using the shipping bills and proof of payment received.

## If the promise is not kept

The duty that was not paid must be paid, with interest. Selling the imported inputs in India instead of using them for exports can bring full duty and further penalties.

DGFT issues notices that change deadlines and procedures, so the current ones should be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: SCOMET in simple words: when an export needs a licence
posts.excerpt: What the SCOMET list is, how to check whether a product is on it, and what happens if it is.
posts.body:
Most goods can be exported without special permission. A small group cannot, because they can be used for both civilian and military purposes. India controls their export through a list called SCOMET, short for Special Chemicals, Organisms, Materials, Equipment and Technologies.

## What the list covers

The list is notified under Appendix 3 to Schedule 2 of the ITC (HS) Classification of Export and Import Items, and is grouped into categories from 0 to 8. It covers chemicals, micro-organisms, materials, electronics, equipment and technology. It also covers software and technical data, not only physical goods.

Most categories are handled by DGFT. Two are handled by other departments: nuclear items by the Department of Atomic Energy, and military items by the Department of Defence Production.

## How to check a product

- Find the product's 8-digit ITC (HS) code, and look for it in the list.
- Compare the technical specifications with the entry, because some items are controlled only above certain limits.
- If the product is on the list, an export authorisation is needed before shipping.
- If the classification is unclear, the exporter can seek the opinion of the authorities, instead of guessing.

## How to apply

The application is made on the DGFT portal, under the licence for SCOMET exports. It needs a valid IEC and papers such as the purchase order, technical details of the item and an end-use and end-user certificate. The application can be sent to other ministries for their views, and if any of them objects, it is rejected.

A standard authorisation is valid for 24 months, and it cannot be transferred to anyone else. Some items can use general authorisations, which have simpler conditions.

## Why it matters

Shipping a SCOMET item without an authorisation is a serious violation. It can lead to penalties under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 and other laws, and to action against the Importer-Exporter Code.

## The list changes

DGFT updates the list from time to time to keep it in line with international export control regimes, and a revised list was notified in 2025. The current list should always be checked before an export.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Duty drawback in simple words: getting customs duty back on exported goods
posts.excerpt: How exporters recover customs duty paid on imported inputs, and the difference between the two types of rate.
posts.body:
An exporter who imports inputs to make goods for export pays customs duty on those inputs. Duty drawback gives that duty back once the finished goods are exported. It is based on section 75 of the Customs Act, 1962 and the drawback rules made under it.

## The two kinds of rate

- **All Industry Rate (AIR).** The government publishes a schedule that gives a fixed refund rate for each product, based on its tariff code. The rate reflects the average duty on the inputs used by the industry.
- **Brand Rate.** If a product is not in the schedule, or the AIR is much lower than the duty actually paid (below about 80% of it), the exporter can apply for a rate worked out from its own inputs. The application goes to the Customs Commissioner, with statements and certificates.

## How to claim an AIR

1. When filing the shipping bill, the exporter declares the AIR serial number for the product.
2. The exporter's bank account and Authorised Dealer code must be registered with customs through ICEGATE, mapped to the port of export. Without this, the drawback cannot be credited.
3. After the export is recorded, the amount is credited straight to the bank account.

## A condition to remember

The export money must be received within the time allowed, usually nine months under RBI rules. If it is not, customs can ask for the drawback back, with interest.

## Drawback and RoDTEP

Drawback refunds customs duty on imported inputs. RoDTEP refunds other taxes built into the cost, such as those on fuel and electricity. They deal with different taxes, but whether both can be claimed on the same goods depends on the rules for that product, so it should be checked.

## Rates change

The drawback schedule is revised from time to time. The rate for the shipping bill date should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: BIS and QCO in simple words: what importers must check before ordering
posts.excerpt: What a Quality Control Order is, how BIS certification works for imported goods, and why the check comes before the purchase order.
posts.body:
Some products cannot be made, imported or sold in India unless they meet an Indian Standard and carry the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) mark. The government makes this compulsory through a Quality Control Order (QCO). It is issued under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016, by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade or by another ministry.

## What a QCO does

A QCO lists a product and the Indian Standard it must meet. From the date given in the order, the product must be certified by BIS, and must carry the mark where the scheme requires it.

## The main routes to certification

- **ISI mark (product certification).** The product is tested against the Indian Standard and the factory is audited. A foreign manufacturer has to go through this for its own factory.
- **Compulsory Registration Scheme (CRS).** Used mainly for electronics and IT goods. The product is tested in a BIS-recognised lab, and a factory audit is usually not needed.

A foreign manufacturer without an office in India has to appoint an Authorised Indian Representative to deal with BIS.

## Why importers must check first

- Customs can hold or reject a shipment that does not have the required certification.
- Goods without it can also face seizure, penalties and limits on sale.
- Certification can take weeks or months, so an order placed first and checked later can leave the goods stuck at the port.

## Steps before placing an order

1. Check whether the product, by its tariff heading and description, is covered by a QCO.
2. Find the Indian Standard and the scheme that apply.
3. Confirm that the foreign supplier holds a valid BIS licence or registration for that product.
4. Check labels and markings against BIS requirements.
5. Keep the licence and test records ready for customs.

## The list keeps changing

New products are added to the QCO list, while some orders have been withdrawn or have had their dates extended in 2025 and 2026. The current order for the product should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Import Export Code (IEC) in simple words: the 10-digit number every importer and exporter needs
posts.excerpt: What an IEC is, who needs it, how it is obtained and why it must be kept updated.
posts.body:
If you want to import or export goods or services as a business in India, you generally need an Import Export Code, called IEC. It is a 10-digit number issued by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992.

## Why it matters

Customs, banks and DGFT use the IEC to identify you. Without it, you normally cannot clear imports or ship exports, and you cannot claim export schemes such as RoDTEP, Advance Authorisation or EPCG.

## Who needs it

- Any business that imports or exports goods in the course of trade.
- Exporters of services may need it to claim benefits under some schemes.
- Certain persons are exempt. For example, imports for personal use, or imports and exports by some government departments. The exemptions are listed in the Foreign Trade Policy, so check them for your case.

## How it is obtained

- The application is made online on the DGFT portal.
- It is linked to the PAN of the business. One PAN can have only one IEC.
- Usually needed: PAN, proof of the business address, a bank detail or cancelled cheque, and a digital signature or Aadhaar-based authentication.
- A government fee applies. The current amount is shown on the portal.

## Keep it alive

- The IEC itself is valid for life, but it must be updated online every year, in the period April to June, even if nothing has changed.
- If it is not updated, the IEC can be deactivated. It can be reactivated after the update.
- Changes such as address, directors or bank details should be updated in the portal when they happen.

## Common mistakes

- Details on the IEC do not match the shipping bill or bill of entry.
- Forgetting the yearly update and finding the code inactive on the day of shipment.
- Using an IEC of another entity.

Rules, fees and procedures change, so the current DGFT portal and Foreign Trade Policy should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: IGCR in simple words: import raw material at a lower duty for your factory
posts.excerpt: How the concessional duty rules for specified end use work, and what a manufacturer must keep in mind.
posts.body:
Some customs notifications give a lower rate of duty on goods, but only if the goods are used for a particular purpose, such as making a specific product. IGCR is the set of rules that lets a manufacturer claim such a lower rate in an organised way.

The full name is the Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty) Rules, 2017. They were later replaced by the Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022, which carry the same idea forward with a more automated process.

## The basic idea

- A notification says that a certain good is charged a lower duty if used for a stated end use.
- The importer registers with customs, giving details of the factory and the goods.
- The goods are imported at the lower duty and used only for the stated purpose.
- The importer keeps records and files periodic statements showing how the goods were used.

## What the importer must do

- Register with the jurisdictional customs office before the import.
- Use the goods only for the declared end use, within the time allowed.
- Maintain a proper account of receipt, use and balance.
- Give the statements and certificates asked for, usually on the customs system.

## What can go wrong

- Goods are used for something else, or are sold without permission. Customs can then demand the duty that was saved, with interest and possibly penalty.
- Records are incomplete, so use cannot be proved.

## IGCR and other schemes

IGCR is different from MOOWR, where duty is deferred, and from Advance Authorisation, where duty is exempt for exports. In IGCR the duty is actually paid, but at a lower rate.

The exact conditions are written in each notification and in the Rules, so those should be read for the goods concerned.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: RoSCTL in simple words: getting back taxes on garment and made-up exports
posts.excerpt: What the Rebate of State and Central Taxes and Levies scheme covers and how a claim is made.
posts.body:
When you export, the exported product should not carry Indian taxes. Most taxes are already refunded through GST. But some State and Central levies, such as taxes on electricity used in manufacture or on fuel, are not refunded that way. RoSCTL refunds these hidden taxes to exporters.

The full name is Rebate of State and Central Taxes and Levies.

## Who gets it

- The scheme is for exports of apparel, garments and made-ups, such as bed linen and towels.
- It is claimed on the shipping bill, so the shipment must be of an eligible product.

## How much

- The rebate is a percentage of the export value (the FOB value). The percentage depends on the product and is given in a rate table issued by the Ministry of Textiles.
- Some products have a cap per unit.

## How it is claimed

- The exporter declares the scheme on the shipping bill. The claim is then processed by customs and paid by electronic scrip or credit, as the current procedure says.
- Proper Harmonised System (HS) code and product description matter, because the rate depends on them.

## Things to remember

- The scheme has been extended from time to time. It runs for a fixed period, so check whether it applies to the date of your shipment.
- It cannot be combined with certain other benefits on the same product, for example RoDTEP. Rules on this are in the scheme notification.
- Rates and conditions can change.

The current rate table and notification should always be checked before claiming.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Special Economic Zones (SEZ) in simple words
posts.excerpt: What an SEZ is, what benefits a unit gets, and the main conditions that come with them.
posts.body:
A Special Economic Zone, or SEZ, is a defined area in India which is treated, for trade and customs, like foreign territory. It is governed by the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005 and its Rules.

## The idea

Businesses set up inside the zone are meant to produce mainly for export. In return they get certain duty and tax advantages, which make Indian exports more competitive.

## Common benefits

- Import of goods needed for the unit, without payment of customs duty.
- Supplies from India into the zone are generally treated as exports, and can be zero-rated under GST.
- Some income tax benefits existed for units, but they were time-limited and have been changed over the years, so the current Income Tax law should be checked.

## Main conditions

- The unit needs approval from the Development Commissioner of the zone, and signs a Letter of Approval.
- It must earn net foreign exchange over the stated period. This is usually checked over a block of five years.
- Goods and services must be used for the authorised operations.
- Records, returns and annual performance reports must be filed.

## Selling in India (DTA)

Goods can be sold from the SEZ into the rest of India, called the Domestic Tariff Area. This is treated like an import, so customs duty is payable on it, according to the rules in force.

## Points to watch

- Misuse of duty-free goods can lead to recovery of the duty with interest and penalty.
- Exemptions are not automatic. Each benefit depends on meeting its condition and following the procedure.

Policy changes happen often, so the current SEZ Rules and notifications should be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Starting a private limited company in India: the basic steps
posts.excerpt: A plain walk through what a private company is and how it is incorporated with the Registrar of Companies.
posts.body:
A private limited company is the most common form of company for a small or growing business. It is a separate legal person. The owners (shareholders) are generally liable only up to the amount unpaid on their shares. It is governed by the Companies Act, 2013.

## Basic requirements

- At least two directors, and at least one of them must be resident in India (stayed in India for 182 days or more in the previous year).
- At least two shareholders. A director can also be a shareholder.
- A registered office address in India.
- A name that is available and is not identical or too similar to an existing company or trademark.
- A digital signature and a Director Identification Number (DIN) for each proposed director.

## The steps in short

- Choose and reserve the name. This is done in the SPICe+ form on the MCA portal.
- Prepare the Memorandum of Association and Articles of Association, which state the objects and the internal rules.
- File the SPICe+ form with its linked forms, which also apply for PAN, TAN and other registrations.
- The Registrar checks the documents. If they are in order, a Certificate of Incorporation is issued, with the company's Corporate Identity Number (CIN).

## After incorporation

- Open a company bank account and bring in the share capital.
- Hold the first board meeting, and appoint the auditor within the time allowed.
- File the declaration for commencement of business as the law requires.
- Every year, file annual returns and financial statements, and hold the annual general meeting. A company that does not comply can face penalties.

## Other options

Depending on the case, a Limited Liability Partnership, One Person Company or a partnership firm may suit better. The choice depends on liability, funding plans, tax and the number of people involved.

Fees, forms and rules are updated from time to time, so the MCA portal should be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Trademark registration in simple words: protect your brand name and logo
posts.excerpt: What a trademark is and how it moves from application to registration in India.
posts.body:
A trademark is a word, name, logo, slogan, shape or colour combination that tells customers whose goods or services they are buying. In India it is protected under the Trade Marks Act, 1999 and registered with the Trade Marks Registry.

## Why register

Registration gives you the exclusive right to use the mark for the goods or services you have registered it for, and the right to sue for infringement. Without registration you may still protect a well-known brand through passing off, but it is harder to prove.

## Steps

- Search first. Check the Registry records for identical or similar marks in your class.
- Choose the class. Goods and services are divided into 45 classes under the Nice classification. The application is made for each relevant class.
- File the application, in Form TM-A, online. It can be made on the basis of use or "proposed to be used".
- Examination. The Registry examines the application and may raise an objection in an examination report. A reply must be filed within the time given.
- Publication. If accepted, the mark is published in the Trade Marks Journal.
- Opposition. Anyone can oppose within four months of publication. If there is opposition, both sides present their case.
- Registration. If there is no opposition, or the opposition fails, the certificate is issued.

## Validity

A registration lasts ten years from the date of application and can be renewed for further periods of ten years, on time and by paying the renewal fee.

## Points to remember

- The symbol TM can be used once you start claiming the mark. The symbol R can be used only after registration.
- A mark that is only descriptive, or too common, may be refused.
- Fees differ for individuals, startups, small enterprises and others.

Procedures and fees change, so the Trade Marks Registry website should be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Customs show cause notice in simple words: what it is and what happens next
posts.excerpt: What a show cause notice means, the stages that follow, and why the reply and records matter.
posts.body:
A show cause notice, called SCN, is a written notice from the customs department. It says that the department thinks something is wrong, such as short payment of duty, wrong classification or a wrong claim of exemption, and asks you to explain why action should not be taken against you.

An SCN is not a final decision. It is the start of a process in which you get a chance to respond.

## What it contains

- The facts the department relies on and the documents behind them.
- The provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 said to be violated. Demands for duty are commonly under section 28, and confiscation or penalty proceedings come under other sections of the Act.
- The amount of duty, interest and penalty proposed.
- The date and officer before whom you should reply.

## Time limits

The law sets time limits within which a notice must be issued, and shorter periods apply when there is no allegation of fraud or wilful misstatement. A notice issued late can be challenged on that ground.

## What to do on receiving one

- Read it fully and note the date for reply. Ask for the relied-upon documents if they were not supplied.
- Collect your records: invoices, bills of entry, contracts, certificates and correspondence.
- Prepare a written reply, covering facts, law and any time-limit objection.
- Ask for a personal hearing. Natural justice requires that you be heard.

## What follows

- The adjudicating officer considers the reply and hearing, and passes an order in writing.
- If the order is against you, an appeal can be filed with the Commissioner (Appeals) within the time allowed, and then to the Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal (CESTAT).
- Some appeals need a pre-deposit of a part of the disputed amount.

## Do not ignore it

If no reply is filed, the officer can decide on the material available. Paying the duty with interest early, where the law allows, can sometimes reduce or close the matter, so the options should be understood before acting.

Every case depends on its facts, and the time limits are strict, so the notice should be examined with the documents in hand.

This post is general information, not legal advice.
